Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

The Bombay High Court on Friday struck down the amendments to Information Technology (IT) Rules allowing the Central government to establish Fact-Check Units. 

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB).

What a Portfolio Cannot Tell You About Itself

How we use the /compelle skill, and what a constructed SaaS and consumer goods book taught us about our own reasoning

Last week I said Compelle is beta-testing the next generation of adversarial reasoning with AI, and that a closed beta of a Claude /compelle skill opens at the end of the month. 

This is the longer version: what the skill does step by step, what happened when we pointed it at a model portfolio, and, most importantly, what it does that a bare Claude Code session cannot.

The problem with asking a model to argue with itself

Ask Claude to "steelman both sides" of a thesis and you get a competent essay. One model, one set of priors, one context window, grading its own homework. 

The Con case is written by the same mind that wrote the Pro case, so it never lands a punch the author did not already see coming. Nothing is at stake, nothing is scored, and nothing is remembered next week.

Compelle changes the structure of the exercise rather than the quality of the prose. Two independent frontier-model debaters take opposite seats on a single motion. Either side may concede outright when its position collapses. Otherwise the transcript goes to a judge panel that must name a winner and the decisive move, in writing. 

Every contest the arena runs on its own schedule enters a public corpus, so the next question you ask can be checked against prior outcomes on adjacent motions. 

Debates you commission through the API are the exception: they are private to your account and never enter that public canon. The /compelle skill is the harness that turns your raw context into that arena and turns the arena's output back into a decision brief.

The workflow, stage by stage:

The skill runs six ordered stages. Each writes an artifact to a run folder; the next stage reads it. No money moves until Stage 4, and then only after every earlier gate has passed.

Stage 1: Interpret. You hand the skill anything: a memo, a decision, a list of tickers and share counts, a draft essay. It classifies the task into one of five modes (decision, thesis, stress test, forecast, sweep), which sets how many motions get written and whether each gets a single debate or a multi-entrant tournament. For the portfolio it chose thesis mode: decompose into load-bearing claims, tournament on the crux, single debates on the rest.

Stage 1.5: Anchor. Before a single motion is written, the skill lists every number the motions will depend on (prices with timestamps, revenue figures, deadlines, market caps) and retrieves each one from a citable source. It writes sources.json with one record per fact: value, unit, as-of date, URL, supporting excerpt, limitations. Sourced observations, your assumptions, your chosen thresholds, and derived values live in separate lists. If a required fact cannot be retrieved, the run records it as unavailable and refuses to commission. The rule is simple: never fill an anchor from memory and present it as current. A debater given a context with no numbers will invent plausible ones, and the run is contaminated before it starts.

Stage 2: Write and lint. Each motion is one neutral, debatable claim with every number supported and every comparison anchored to a stated baseline. A deterministic linter then blocks hard failures: missing as-of date, an unsupported figure, a forecast without a resolution date and criteria, a comparison without a reference. Softer flags trigger a wording-risk pass, where the skill estimates how much advantage the phrasing alone hands one seat. The test we use is the seat swap: imagine Pro and Con reversed. If your expectation of the winner changes because of the words rather than the substance, rewrite. Anything above a 65/35 wording-only advantage stays in review until rewritten or explicitly accepted.

Stage 2.5: Historical baseline. The skill syncs the public arena corpus and searches for prior motions nearest to yours, reporting Pro and Con wins, draws, voids, denominators, and date coverage. This is a prior on how the arena has treated this shape of argument, not a probability about the world, and the brief says so. The corpus contains only the arena's own games. Nothing you have paid to commission is in it, and nothing you commission will be added to it, so your baseline is never contaminated by your own prior runs and your questions are never exposed to the next user's search.

Stage 3: Quote and dry run. A live quote for every motion with its exact configuration, per-order ceilings, the aggregate ceiling, and the full commission payloads, printed for your approval. You approve one aggregate cap per run. If the plan exceeds it, the skill shows the plan and stops.

Stage 4: Commission, poll, validate. Only lint-passing motions within budget are submitted. Each order carries a persisted idempotency key so a retry after a dropped connection returns the existing order rather than charging twice. Results are validated at the boundary: a fulfilled order with missing games or a malformed transcript is quarantined, not silently digested.

Stage 5: Digest and novelty. Per motion: the tally, any concessions with the turn number, judge agreement and dissent, and the decisive-move sentences. Then a second pass reads every transcript and classifies each credited argument as already in your context, a rephrasing, a new argument, or an unsupported new fact. A validator rejects any classification whose cited excerpt does not appear verbatim in the cited turn. This is the stage that surfaces the unknown knowns.

Stage 6: Brief and ledger. One brief that separates sourced facts from your assumptions, arena outcomes from truth, judge agreement from dissent, robust conclusions from wording-sensitive ones. Resolvable motions are recorded in a prediction ledger with criteria fixed now, and scored later against realized prices. Criteria are never edited after recording.

What the model portfolio taught us:

To test the system we built a $1M book, 25 names, half fallen-angel SaaS and half manufacturing and consumer goods, large-cap biased, round lots. Deliberately generic. The interesting question was not whether the portfolio was good but whether the system could tell us what we would have to believe for it to be good.

Lesson 1: A list of tickers is a thesis in disguise, and the system can read it back to you. Handed nothing but symbols and share counts, the skill inferred the strategy (mean reversion on software multiples, hedged by cash-generative industrials) and then decomposed it into the claims the strategy cannot survive without. For the SaaS half:

Enterprise software seat-based revenue will not decline in aggregate through 2028 despite agentic AI adoption. This was identified as the crux and got the tournament.
Software forward P/E below the S&P 500 multiple is a mean-reverting anomaly rather than a durable repricing.
Private-credit stress in software-backed loans will not force distressed equity issuance at any large-cap SaaS name in the next 18 months.
Cybersecurity and observability vendors will keep a valuation premium over application software through 2027.

None of these were written down anywhere. All of them were implied by the weights. That is the first thing the system does better than a human reviewer: it refuses to let a position hide inside an allocation.

Lesson 2: The crux was not where we thought. We assumed the SaaS bet lived or died on valuation. The decomposition put the pricing-unit question first: not "will revenue fall" but "will the market pay for revenue whose pricing unit is being abandoned." Once you see that framing, the valuation motion becomes downstream of it. Multiple compression is a symptom; seat decoupling is the disease.

Lesson 3: Run every conclusion twice, in opposite words. The compression thesis went to the arena as a pair: once as "SaaS multiples will compress further from here" and once inverted as "SaaS multiples will expand from here," with an identical anchored context and an explicit rule for how a tie is scored. The digest normalizes the two verdicts to a single canonical direction and labels the pair robust if they agree and wording-sensitive if they split. That label is the point of the exercise. A conclusion that survives its own inversion is a claim about software. A conclusion that flips with the phrasing is a claim about the phrasing, which means it was never a conclusion at all, and no amount of confidence in the memo changes that. We now treat any single-framing verdict as unfinished work.

Lesson 4: Concessions are the loudest signal, and the easiest to misread. When a debater abandons its seat mid-contest, it is telling you the position could not be held against a motivated opponent with the same facts. That is worth more than a split panel on the same motion. But a concession in one game is not a verdict on the motion, so the digest always reports three things together: which side conceded, which side benefited, and which side won the majority of decided games. Reading only the first of those is how you turn one bad afternoon for Con into a portfolio decision.

Lesson 5: Silence is information. Half the book was industrials and consumer goods, chosen as ballast. The decomposition of that half produced fewer load-bearing claims and none we could honestly call a crux, which is what you would hope from a hedge. It is also what you would see from a hedge nobody had examined closely. The brief distinguishes the two by naming, for every claim, whether it was contested, conceded, or never put to the arena, so a quiet position stays marked as quiet rather than quietly promoted to safe.

What this adds beyond Claude Code

Claude Code, on its own, can decompose a thesis, write both sides, and produce a readable memo. It does all of this inside one model's priors with no external check and no cost to being wrong.

The /compelle skill adds five things a single-model session structurally cannot provide:

Independent adversaries. The Con case is written by an agent whose only objective is to beat the Pro case. It does not share the author's blind spots because it did not read the author's mind. The arguments the novelty pass surfaced as new were new because no cooperative model would have generated them.

A judge that must show its work. The panel names a winner and the decisive move in writing. You get the sentence that turned the game, with a game and turn reference you can verify against the transcript. That is the raw material for revising a thesis, and it does not exist in a self-critique.

Concession as a signal. A debater that abandons its position mid-contest is doing something a prompted model never does: admitting it lost. The Δ is the closest thing to a costly signal you can get from a language model.

A historical corpus, and a private ledger. The arena's own verdicts are public. Before spending on a new question, the skill checks how the arena has treated adjacent motions. Nothing in a chat session accumulates; the arena does. Your commissioned debates, by contrast, stay out of that public record entirely: the motion, the context you supplied, the transcripts, and the verdict are returned to you and to no one else. You get the benefit of the canon without contributing your thesis to it.

A scored ledger. Resolvable forecasts are recorded with fixed criteria and resolved later against realized prices. Over time you learn whether arena verdicts on your questions have any correspondence to outcomes, which is the only calibration that matters and the one no chat interface offers.

Around all of that, the skill enforces discipline that a human analyst usually skips: sourced anchors before motions, a linter before spending, idempotent orders, validated results, and a brief that keeps arena outcomes and truth in separate sentences.¹

What happens next:

The closed beta opens at the end of the month for early adopters. If you run a book, a fund, or a research desk and want to see what your positions are actually asserting, reply to the original post or write to us. Bring a memo or a ticker list. The system will tell you what you have to believe.

¹ Limitations the brief always states: an arena verdict is which case was argued better under published rules, never established truth and never a calibrated probability; a judge seat may share a model family with a debater, and in-family bias is a known limitation of the method; six games on a motion is a small sample for a win rate; historical arena outcomes on adjacent motions are a prior on the arena, not on the world; every number a debater introduces that is not in the sourced context is flagged for verification before reuse; API-commissioned debates are private to the purchasing account and are not added to the public corpus, so the historical baseline reflects arena-scheduled games only.

I submitted a complaint to BOP, DOJ OIG, and Rick Scott.

The message I sent:

I write concerning the confinement of Emory Andrew Tate and Tristan Tate at the Federal Detention Center, Miami. They are held on a United Kingdom extradition warrant. They are not serving a United States sentence and have not been convicted of a U.S. crime.

Federal pretrial-style detention is governed by the Due Process Clause, not the Eighth Amendment standard applied to convicted prisoners. Under Bell v. Wolfish, 441 U.S. 520 (1979), conditions or restrictions amount to unconstitutional punishment if they are imposed with an expressed intent to punish, or if they are not reasonably related to a legitimate nonpunitive purpose—security, order, or ensuring appearance—or are excessive in relation to that purpose.

Bureau of Prisons regulations independently require that Special Housing Unit conditions meet basic humane standards, including sanitary, well-ventilated, and appropriately heated quarters; a mattress, blankets, pillow, and linens; hygiene items; and ordinarily at least five hours of exercise per week. See 28 C.F.R. § 541.31.

Public statements attributed to the detainees and their counsel describe more than two months in SHU; continued segregation after inmates placed there for violence were returned to general population in about seven days; a recent move to a cell alleged to lack air conditioning and hot water and to have a visible cockroach infestation; limited recreation and sunlight; inadequate bedding; exposure to chemical spray without decontamination; and hostile treatment after complaints, including an incident over extra books. Facility-wide reports of heat, pests, and plumbing problems at FDC Miami give those allegations a context beyond a single high-profile account.

Administrative or “protective” labels do not end the inquiry. Prolonged SHU detention of unconvicted extradition detainees, without a time-limited, reviewable, individualized security finding, combined with conditions alleged to fall below the Bureau’s own SHU rules and to have worsened after public complaint, supports an inference of punishment in fact.

I do not ask that these men receive privileges unavailable to other detainees. I ask that their housing be measured against Bell and 28 C.F.R. § 541.31: a documented, current justification for SHU placement; sanitary and climate-adequate cells; required exercise; and no retaliatory downgrade of conditions.

Please review their classification, cell assignment, and conditions of confinement and correct any practice that is punitive or that fails Bureau regulations.

🚨 STOP ASKING AI TO “SUMMARIZE THIS PDF.”

That’s barely 10% of what you can do.

text: @IkerBasanti @EvanAKilgore Is it really a “sale” if it’s money from our taxes anyways? Sounds like robbing Peter to pay Paul, but it’s really just robbing us to pay us. Weird.

Hi KC :) 

Israel can write its own check because it is not a poor client state. It is a rich, high-tech country with a huge weapons-export business.
How Israel can pay:

•  Its economy is first-world: high GDP per head, big tax base, deep capital markets.
•  Its defense companies are exporters, not pets. Elbit, Rafael, IAI sell worldwide. Recent years were record export years (on the order of $15 billion a year). That cash is Israeli, not American.

•  After October 7 Israel raised its own defense budget. FMF used to look huge next to Israel’s military spending. Now Israel’s own wallet is the main wallet; the U.S. grant is the topping.
•  Netanyahu has even said out loud he wants to draw the cash aid down toward zero and call it partnership, not allowance. That only makes sense if Jerusalem thinks it can float the bill.
So “can they afford it?” — yes, more than in 1980 or 2000. The grant is leverage and a bulk discount on U.S. kit, not oxygen.
Why the U.S. still likes the deal (the part your friends asked about)

Washington does not “need” Israel the way a customer needs a sole supplier. It wants three things that are hard to buy on the open market:

1.  A buyer that already lives on the U.S. catalog F-35s, U.S. munitions, U.S. engines. Every extra Israeli order keeps those lines hot and the unit price down for the Pentagon. That is business. Not charity.
2.  Tech that went the other way Trophy on tanks, Iron Dome co-produced with Raytheon, certain drones, cyber, targeting. Israeli firms open U.S. shops so they can touch FMF dollars — and U.S. primes get the American-made version. Two-way capture.
3.  Gear used in real fights The U.S. still does its own tests. What Israel adds is high-tempo combat use of U.S.-origin systems and the after-action data. That is valuable. It is not the same as “America cannot design weapons without Israel.”

X-short
Israel can pay because it got rich and it sells weapons to the world, not just to itself.
The U.S. keeps writing the gift card because the card is spent in Ohio and Texas, the customer already speaks American weapons, and some of the best add-ons (Trophy, Iron Dome class kit) came back across the ocean.
That is a joint order book, not a food-stamp line.
Ending the old “spend 26% in Israel” rule was the U.S. saying: if we fund it, the factory stays here. Israel saying it can wean off the cash is Israel saying: our own exports and budget can carry more of the load. Both can be true at once.

DELHI SIR: 33 LAKH VOTERS UNDER SCRUTINY, BUT WHERE IS THE TRANSPARENCY?

33 lakh Delhi voters are being asked to prove themselves. Yet the public is being denied a basic piece of information: who has been issued these notices, and on what precise grounds?

The ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Delhi's electoral rolls has put roughly 33.1 lakh voters under scrutiny. Of these, 19.33 lakh have reportedly been flagged by ECI software for 11 categories of “logical discrepancies”, while another 13.79 lakh are classified as “unmapped”. 

These are not trivial numbers.

Delhi began this exercise with an electorate of around 1.45 crore. The draft roll published on August 31 contains about 97.5 lakh voters whose enumeration forms were digitised. 

THE FIRST TRANSPARENCY QUESTION

The ECI's own SIR instructions reproduced in the letter sent by Anjali Bharadwaj and Amrita Johri to the Delhi Chief Electoral Officer say that lists of electors to whom notices have been issued are to be published and made accessible.

Yet reporting on the current Delhi exercise says the full list of flagged electors has not been uploaded publicly; the names are accessible to Booth Level Officers through their official application. 

That creates a legitimate democratic question:

If a voter is being formally flagged by the election machinery, why should the voter—and the public—have to operate in an information vacuum?

Transparency cannot mean merely telling citizens, “You have been flagged.”

They must be told why.

THE SECOND QUESTION: WHAT EXACTLY IS A “DISCREPANCY”?

This is even more important.

The 19.33 lakh voters were not necessarily found to be fraudulent. They were flagged by software because data did not reconcile across electoral records. A software flag is not, by itself, proof that a voter is ineligible or that an electoral entry is false. 

The reported 11 categories include things such as:

unusual parent-child age gaps;

more than six children linked to one parent;

less than nine months between two children;

discrepancies in parent names;

changes in relationship classification;

age differences between successive electoral rolls;

mismatches in the elector's or father's name. 

Some of these may be genuine anomalies.

But a database anomaly is not the same thing as voter fraud.

And that distinction is fundamental.

WHY PUBLIC DISCLOSURE MATTERS

Imagine a citizen receiving a notice saying:

Your electoral record has a “discrepancy.”

But the citizen doesn't know:

Which field?
Which previous record?
What mismatch?
What rule triggered the flag?
What evidence is required?
Who authorised the algorithmic classification?

That is not meaningful procedural transparency.

The ECI's own stated objective of SIR is clear: no eligible citizen should be left out and no ineligible person should be included. 

That objective cannot be achieved merely by detecting discrepancies.

It requires due process, transparency, an opportunity to respond, and an auditable trail of decisions.

AND THIS IS NOT AN ABSTRACT CONCERN

Delhi has already seen serious questions around the pre-SIR electoral-roll changes. The CEO's office has said that names were not deleted without inquiry and an opportunity to be heard, while reporting has highlighted substantial changes in the electorate before the formal SIR. 

That makes transparency during the current verification phase even more important.

Source/document: Letter dated September 13, 2026, from Anjali Bharadwaj & Amrita Johri to the Chief Electoral Officer, Delhi, reproduced in the supplied images.

Independent research: Current reporting corroborates the approximately 33.1 lakh voters under scrutiny, 19.33 lakh logical-discrepancy flags and 13.79 lakh unmapped .

Official ECI voter portal: [ECI Voter Services](https://t.co/sV2CWCJP8L)

Fair Use: This post uses publicly available material for criticism, commentary, research and public-interest discussion.

#DimaagiNaxal #Resistance #UnitedResistance

When millions of citizens are being subjected to scrutiny, the scrutiny itself must be scrutinised.

THE PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLE

Clean electoral rolls are essential.

Removing genuinely ineligible entries is legitimate.

Correcting errors is legitimate.

But democracy cannot demand proof from citizens while withholding information about the basis on which they were flagged.

The Election Commission has enormous constitutional responsibility because the electoral roll is the gateway to the most fundamental democratic act:

the right to vote.

So the demand is neither complicated nor partisan:

Publish the notice list.
Publish the rules.
Publish the categories.
Publish the instructions and software criteria.
Tell every flagged voter exactly what discrepancy has been identified.
Give every citizen a fair opportunity to answer.

Because electoral integrity and transparency are not competing goals.

Transparency is what makes electoral integrity credible.

A voter should never have to prove their existence to an opaque algorithm.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Okay. Let me walk you through what happened.

On 31 August 2026, Malesela Teffo arrived at the Johannesburg High Court during Cat Matlala's attempted murder trial.

He was not on the case. He was not representing anyone. He walked in unannounced and asked to intervene — as a "friend of the court," or through his Pro Bono Foundation, claiming constitutional violations.

Judge Cassim Moosa told him to produce proof of readmission from the LPC or the High Court. Teffo could not.

The application was stood down.

Then the police arrived.

Here is what you need to understand before the headlines write themselves.

1. Teffo is not a lawyer anymore.

He was admitted as an advocate in 2009. But in September 2022, the Pretoria High Court struck him off the roll following an application by the Legal Practice Council.

The court cited serious professional misconduct: misappropriating client funds, taking briefs directly from clients without instructing attorneys, misleading courts, breaching court orders.

These were not allegations. These were findings of a court.

And in July 2026, he was acquitted of six criminal charges — assault, fraud-related matters, incidents from 2023. The LPC made clear: acquittal does not restore your right to practise. An acquittal says the state did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It does not erase a striking-off order.

He remains struck off. He is not entitled to appear in court or offer legal services.

2. The warrant was already in the system.

The LPC confirmed a warrant of arrest existed, stemming from a prior contempt finding. A 2023/2024 court order declared him in contempt of the original striking-off order, with a suspended 12-month imprisonment sentence if he complied.

Police had previously been unable to locate him.

Then he walked into a courtroom.

3. Now the context matters.

The trial he interrupted was Cat Matlala's — the same Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala who won the R360 million SAPS medical tender that was later confirmed as irregular expenditure, with at least R50 million already paid before cancellation.

Matlala has been arrested on corruption and fraud charges. The charges against Police Commissioner Masemola linked to that tender were just dropped by the NPA.

Teffo is not a random bystander in this story.

He is a former defence counsel in the Senzo Meyiwa trial who gained prominence through that high-profile exposure. He positioned himself as a constitutional watchdog. And he showed up at the courtroom of a man whose tender was built on the same rot that the Madlanga Commission is currently mapping.

4. Here is the uncomfortable part.

A struck-off advocate appearing during a corruption trial does not raise the same question it would if the accused were a nobody.

When you remove yourself from the rolls of legal practitioners, when you are in contempt of the order that removed you, when a warrant is already circulating — and then you choose that moment to walk into that courtroom and ask to intervene...

The timing does not read like constitutional activism.

It reads like someone who knows which courtroom will get cameras.

5. That does not mean the constitutional questions he raised are wrong.

It does not mean the accused should not get a fair trial. It does not mean the state cannot abuse process.

But it does mean we should be clear about what this is.

It is not an advocate defending the rule of law.

It is a man who has been told by two separate courts that he cannot practise law, walking into a high-profile corruption trial and asking to be heard.

The judge did not hear him. The police did.

The uncomfortable truth:

The rule of law does not need protectors who are themselves subject to warrants.

A struck-off advocate appearing in court is not a constitutional crisis.

It is a man who forgot that the order striking him off was not a suggestion.

And the warrant that finally found him was not new.

It had been waiting.

#Teffo #CatMatlala #MadlangaCommission

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
I was stationed at a military training facility in New Mexico, less than forty-eight hours from completing an eight-month rotation. When Maya’s name appeared on my phone, I assumed she had woken from a bad dream or simply missed her father.

Then I heard her shallow, broken breathing.

“Daddy,” she whispered. “I’m in the hospital.”

I stood so quickly that my chair struck the barracks floor. “Maya, where are you?”

“In El Paso,” she said. “Everything hurts.”

I had spent twelve years in tactical service, trained to stay composed in circumstances most people never see. But nothing prepares a parent for the sound of a child trying not to cry because she is afraid of making her father worry.

“Breathe slowly, sweetheart,” I told her. “Tell me who hurt you.”

There was a long silence.

“Uncle Ross and Uncle Ethan.”

They were my ex-wife Veronica’s brothers. The afternoon before, they had arrived drunk at the Vance family estate in San Jeronimo, where the Vance name carried more influence than any local official seemed willing to admit.

Maya had spilled soda on Ross’s new leather boots.

That was all it took.

“They brought me to the garage,” she said.

My hands went cold. “What happened there?”

“Ross opened the truck,” Maya whispered. “He took out the tire iron.”

Then she gave me the detail that would stay with me long after every court hearing ended.

“I was calling for Mommy. She was standing at the second-floor window. She looked at me, Daddy… and then she pulled the curtain shut.”

A pediatric nurse took the phone when Maya began struggling to breathe. Twelve hours later, I walked into the Children’s Hospital trauma unit in uniform and met Dr. Karina Sterling outside my daughter’s room.

She did not soften the truth. Maya had serious fractures in both arms, broken ribs, a shattered left femur, and injured fingers from trying to shield herself.

“Her body will heal,” Dr. Sterling said. “But her recovery will take much longer than that.”

Through the window, I saw my daughter surrounded by IV lines and soft casts. Every part of me wanted to storm the Vance estate and make someone answer for what they had done.

I did not.

Arthur Vance, my former father-in-law, owned the region’s largest timber and logistics operation. His finance company held mortgages and business loans throughout the town, he funded local campaigns, and Chief of Police Hector Miller ate dinner at his estate most Sundays.

The Vances believed their money made them untouchable. My divorce from Veronica had taught me that they treated custody orders, boundaries, and other people’s rights as inconveniences.

Four days later, Pauline Vance called me while I sat beside Maya’s bed.

“Look who finally decided to play father,” she said with a laugh. “Don’t waste money on lawyers, Mark. Your former brothers-in-law won’t spend a single hour in jail.”

I stayed silent while she continued.

“My husband owns the police, the council, and half the judges. Take the girl when she is discharged and be grateful we let you have her.”

Then her voice sharpened.

“Ross says if you create a public scene, he’ll finish what he started.”

She hung up.

text:
What Pauline did not know was that the call had been recorded. During the custody fight years earlier, my attorney had advised me to document every interaction with the Vance family, and I had never stopped.

I sent the audio to my former commanding officer, Colonel Gabriel Sterling.

“Do not give them the street fight they expect,” he told me. “Document everything, protect Maya, and get this case out of their jurisdiction.”

That night, the Vance-owned news station claimed Maya had suffered an accidental fall from a tree.

Then my phone received a message from an unlisted number.

It contained a six-minute video and only four words:

I saw everything happen.

The footage showed Ross beside his pickup truck, holding the tire iron. Ethan was closing the driveway gate while Maya crawled backward across the concrete.

Up at the second-floor window, Veronica watched her daughter scream for help.

Then she reached for the curtain and pulled it closed.

A second message appeared immediately.

My name is Renee. I’m sixteen. Ross is my father, Maya is my cousin

—and Maya was not the first.

I watched Renee’s video twice. I hated every second of it, but I needed to know exactly what the recording showed and what could be used to protect Maya.

The footage had been taken from an upstairs bedroom, its frame shaking slightly in Renee’s hands. Ross removed the tire iron from the truck bed, Ethan secured the automatic gate, and Maya tried to crawl toward the back patio.

Then the camera caught Veronica at the window.

My daughter looked up at her mother, begging for help. Veronica watched for a moment before drawing the curtain shut.

I made four encrypted copies of the video. One went into a secure cloud vault, one to my family attorney, one to the State Attorney General’s Special Victims Unit, and one through formal military channels to State Police Internal Affairs.

The local police report had called Maya’s injuries a “domestic playground accident.” I wanted no chance for Chief Miller or anyone connected to Arthur Vance to erase the truth again.

Renee agreed to give a formal deposition if the state placed her under immediate witness protection. When I met her at the state precinct, she did not look like the daughter of a powerful, violent man.

She looked like a terrified sixteen-year-old who had spent years measuring every word she said.
“My dad grabbed my phone and made me delete the original video,” she told investigators. “He didn’t know it synced automatically to another account.”

The investigator asked her what she meant when she said Maya was not the first.

Renee’s face went still. “Three years ago, they hurt another boy in the same garage. His name was Mateo. His father worked at my grandfather’s mill.”

“What happened to him?” the prosecutor asked.

“Grandfather’s people told everyone he ran away.”

That was when the case stopped being only about the people who had hurt my daughter. It became an investigation into the system that had protected them.

The State Corruption Task Force examined the police database and found two separate versions of Maya’s incident report. The original described injuries consistent with an assault involving a blunt object.

Hours later, someone using Chief Miller’s credentials replaced it with a report claiming Maya had fallen at home.

Rezaul, a final-year https://t.co/NMjOF3Lwxa student at #AliahUniversity and a resident of Hooghly district’s #Meshera village, was returning from the #BishwaIjtema religious gathering in #Bangladesh along with four friends. The group had boarded a local train from #Gede station to Sealdah when the incident happened.

According to Rezaul, trouble began when a passenger asked him to remove his trolley bag from the luggage rack. He complied without protest, but soon after, a group of men attempted to force him out of his seat. When he resisted, they hurled communal slurs, calling him a “#Bangladeshi.”

“A man named Ajay taunted me, saying, ‘What drove you out of Bangladesh? You’ve come to invade India,’” Rezaul told to media. “I told them I am an Indian citizen, but about a dozen people surrounded me and started attacking me.”

For nearly an hour, Rezaul was repeatedly punched and kicked. His cap was forcibly removed, his hair and beard were pulled, and he was subjected to verbal abuse. At one point, some attackers allegedly urged others to throw him off the moving train.

His friend, Sajid Mirza, attempted to record the assault but was threatened. “They snatched my phone and warned me that if I made a video, they would throw me off the train,” Sajid said. “They accused us of being uneducated militants destroying the country.”

After the attack, Rezaul sought medical treatment before attempting to lodge a complaint at Haripal police station. However, officers allegedly refused to register his case. He later approached the Sealdah Government Railway Police (GRP) on February 5, where his complaint was finally accepted.

A case has been filed under sections 115(2), 299, 351(2), and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), and railway police have launched an investigation. “We are looking into the matter, and appropriate legal action will be taken,” a police official said.

The attack has triggered widespread condemnation. Prominent lawyer and Left MP Bikash Ranjan Bhattacharya linked the incident to growing communal polarization. “This is not an isolated case. Such acts are happening in states governed by #RSS-backed politics,” he wrote on social media. “Over the past decade, West Bengal has been influenced by RSS ideology, fueling religious divisions. A strong secular movement is needed to break this cycle.”

ISF MLA Peerzada Nawsad Siddique questioned the attackers’ motives: “Was Rezaul assaulted simply because he wore a cap and had a beard? This cannot happen in a democracy.”

Human rights groups, including the Association for Protection of Democratic Rights (APDR), also condemned the attack. “This is just the tip of the iceberg. Political parties and sections of the media have turned the state into a communal battleground,” said APDR General Secretary Ranjit Sur.

Mohammad Kamruzzaman of the All Bengal Minority Youth Federation (ABMYF) pointed to a disturbing trend. “Muslim youth have been attacked on trains before. If no action is taken, such incidents will continue,” he warned.

Journalist and activist Moktar Hossain Mondal blamed communal narratives for escalating violence. “Years ago, people were shocked to hear about such attacks on minorities in trains. Now, it’s becoming disturbingly common,” he said.

AP Police impersonated the FBI

Subject: Request for Investigation - Andhra Pradesh Police Officer Identified “FBI” as Requesting Organization in X/Twitter Law-Enforcement Request Concerning a U.S. Citizen

To:
Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
The Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)
@FBI @FBIDirectorKash @FBITampa @TheJusticeDept  
U.S. Department of Justice

Dear Director / Appropriate Federal Officials:

I am a United States citizen residing in the United States. I respectfully submit this complaint and request for review concerning an apparent misrepresentation of U.S. federal law-enforcement identity in connection with a social-media investigation initiated by the Andhra Pradesh Police in India.

I. Summary of the complaint

I recently received a notification from X Support concerning a law-enforcement request submitted to X regarding my X account.
The X communication initially stated that the request had been submitted by the “FBI.”

However, X subsequently provided an important correction. X expressly stated:

“However, this request did not come from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI)”

X further stated that the request actually came from the Andhra Pradesh Police and identified the submitting individual as:

Name: A V Bramham
Position: Inspector of Police
Organization entered by requester: FBI
Email: guntururbansp-ap@gov.in
Location: Guntur, Andhra Pradesh, India
Country: India

X further stated:
“it is unclear why the Andhra Pradesh Police wrote ‘FBI’ as the sender organization.”
I have preserved the X communication and can provide the original notification and screenshot as evidence.
II. Why I am requesting U.S. government review
I fully recognize that foreign law-enforcement agencies may communicate with U.S. companies through legitimate international law-enforcement cooperation channels.
The issue here is different.

According to X’s own records, an Andhra Pradesh Police official submitted the request, but the requesting organization was entered as “FBI.”

I therefore respectfully request that the appropriate U.S. authorities determine:

Whether the FBI had any involvement whatsoever in this request to X.

Whether any FBI office, agent, liaison officer, or other U.S. government agency authorized, participated in, or communicated with Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my X account.
Whether the Andhra Pradesh Police official knowingly or inadvertently represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting the request to X.

Whether the use of “FBI” as the requesting organization was intended to obtain greater credibility, priority, cooperation, disclosure, restriction, or removal of content from X.

Whether X received any other law-enforcement request from Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account in which the FBI was similarly identified.

Whether this conduct implicates any U.S. federal criminal, civil-rights, cyber, impersonation, transnational-repression, or other federal jurisdiction.

Whether the conduct should be referred to another appropriate federal authority for investigation.
III. First Amendment / transnational-repression concern
The underlying matter concerns social-media content posted on X and alleged violations of Indian law.
I am particularly concerned because I am a U.S. citizen residing in the United States, and the governmental action concerns my online speech and political commentary.
I understand that the United States cannot simply disregard legitimate foreign criminal investigations. However, I am requesting that U.S. authorities determine whether a foreign law-enforcement agency has attempted to use the identity or authority of a U.S. federal agency to influence or restrict constitutionally protected activity occurring in the United States.
The FBI itself recognizes transnational repression as an issue that may affect people in the United States and specifically directs individuals who believe they have been affected by transnational repression to report the matter to the FBI.
IV. Request for preservation and investigation of evidence
I respectfully request that the appropriate agency consider preserving and/or obtaining, where legally appropriate:
the original law-enforcement request submitted by Andhra Pradesh Police to X;

all metadata associated with that request;

the identity and authentication information associated with the requester;

the date and time of submission;

all representations made by the requester concerning his identity and governmental organization;
any attachments, legal documents, FIRs, court orders, or other materials submitted to X;

any subsequent communications between X and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning my account;
any communications between U.S. government agencies and Andhra Pradesh Police concerning this matter; and
any evidence showing whether “FBI” was entered intentionally or accidentally.
V. Request for clarification from the FBI
I respectfully request confirmation of the following:
Did the FBI have any involvement in, authorization of, or knowledge of this particular request to X?
If the answer is no, I respectfully request that the FBI consider whether the circumstances warrant investigation or referral concerning the apparent use of the FBI’s identity by a foreign law-enforcement official.
VI. Good-faith submission
I am not asking the U.S. government to interfere with a legitimate Indian criminal investigation.
My request is narrower:
I am asking the United States government to determine whether an Indian police official represented himself or his agency as the FBI when submitting a law-enforcement request concerning a U.S. citizen’s social-media account, and whether that conduct violated any U.S. law or raised a transnational-repression or foreign-government intimidation concern.

I am prepared to provide the original X communication, screenshots, account information, relevant posts, and any notices received from Andhra Pradesh Police.

I respectfully request that this complaint be logged, reviewed, and referred to the appropriate federal authority if the receiving office does not have jurisdiction.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Respectfully,

U.S. Citizen

Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

text:
Anthropic Is Building a Huge Surveillance System to Spy on Anti-AI Activists and Predict Their Activities | Joe Wilkins, Futurism

With opposition to AI continuing to grow, a top AI lab is building out a massive surveillance apparatus meant to keep a close eye on dissenters and predict when the next groundswell of protest might occur.

News of Anthropic’s system was first reported by the American Prospect, which spoke with Anthropic senior security officials and indexed job postings to get an understanding of the dragnet.

On top of keeping tabs on protests in the vicinity of Anthropic offices, the publication notes that the AI lab is taking a “pre-crime” approach to watching for potential civil unrest.

To give an example, the Prospect points out an incident shared by Anthropic security operations managers Keon Ellison and Zach Melvin, alongside James Neufeld, CEO of risk detection company Samdesk.

“Last year we had an executive travel into a major city when we received some intelligence through Samdesk about a planned protest,” Ellison said candidly. After the scheduled protest was moved up an hour due to a mix-up with police permits, the security chief said that “Samdesk gave us about 60 minutes of advanced notice that the protest organizers had moved the timeline.”

“That extra hour was critical,” Ellison continued. “Without it our executives would have departed their meetings, they would have ran right into the heart of the disruption. What could have been a high-stress situation was really mitigated through early detection through Samdesk and giving us that information.”

Outside of anticipating protests, there were also cases where Anthropic reported conversations held with its AI chatbot Claude to police. Though there have been calls to increase safety guardrails on large language models, Anthropic’s approach sounds bizarre.

As the San Francisco Standard reported in August, Anthropic reported a San Francisco man to the cops after he told Claude he was holding a rifle, and had the company’s CEO Dario Amodei “in his sights.” Yet when Anthropic reported the conversation to Bay Area police, the company refused to provide the man’s chat logs — as the Prospect observes, essentially reporting the man without sharing any tangible evidence of misconduct.

“The goal,” as Anthropic’s security manager said in the interview, “would be transforming operations from reactive information to gathering proactive and predictive and preventative threat engagement and management. That’s the kind of operational maturity that makes sense for protecting high-value targets in any industry.”

69A. Section 69A in The Information Technology Act, 2000 
Power to issue directions for blocking for public access of any information through any computer resource.-

1. text:
Most of you want to know what all transpired in between the ‘account withheld in India’ and the final restoration of my account. 

So here’s a quick summary. Please share so that others can take the same recourse, if need be, coz the govt seems in no mood to spare any content critical of it.

On 19th March at 12:23 AM my account was withheld in India.

Very next day, I had a conversation with @SupriyaShrinate and she told me that 12 other accounts met the same fate. She did a live session and addressed media the very same day. That highlighted the issue. The wire, Quint and alt news reported the news.

I swiftly responded to MeitY on 19th March at 4:16 AM enquiring the cause that led to this removal under section 69A. ( Haven’t received any response yet )

Next I consulted with @NakulGandhi511 upon the recommendation of @iArpitSpeaks as he had earlier met with similar fate and got his account back.

Nakul sir guided me for a week and introduced me with @apar1984 who runs @internetfreedom . 

He took over my case pro bono ( for free ) and guided me accordingly. 

On 1st of April I finally filed my writ petition. The notary, wakalatnama was all new to me coz I had never been in court till this date but barring that I had to do nothing. 

Every response, every draft was given to me by @namanbasoyaa who works with Apar sir. 

I got my listing on 6th of April with the honr Judge Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav. 

He didn’t even waste 10 mins and ordered a restore provided that the posts that warranted an action against me shall stay unblocked until the committee level hearing of MeitY ( It’s not scheduled yet )

In fact I still don’t have the blocking order that necessitated such an action against me that is ultra vires of the constitution. Section 69A doesn’t permit govt to remove pre-emotive post based on speculation and that’s exactly what govt effectively did by withholding my entire account not some posts. 

Also big thanks to my followers who stood with me. Some used VPN just to stay connected. I’m indebted to all of you and IFF and Apar sir in particular. 

Taking this opportunity to urge the govt to remove ban from other accounts as well folllwing the same precedence used in mine and @DrNimoYadav ’s case.

FoS needs to be supreme. Taking down post is wrong in itself but an entire account that took years of cultivating is just brutal and uncalled for. 

May better sense prevails. Peace ✌🏽

text:
Dear @raghav_chadha ,

I know you are doing very well in Parliament by raising small issues that were ignored by most Members of Parliament but have a bigger impact.

I am writing this post regarding an account lien and bank freeze by the Cyber Police of India.

In my case, the issue started when I received a message from my bank branch stating that my account had received a police notice of lien of 6000 rupees. I immediately went to my bank branch and asked them why my account had a lien of 6000 rupees. They followed some procedure and gave me a printout which contained the acknowledgement of my lien. One of the bank employees told me that I should contact the cyber police mentioned on the paper and provide them with the details of the 6000 rupees, such as where it came from and for what reason. However, they did not give me any specific reason why my bank account had received the lien.

Later, I checked my bank statement to find the details of the 6000 rupees transaction and noticed that my case was reported on 6 December 2025, and I had received a transaction of 6000 rupees on the same date. I remember that my neighbour had sent me this 6000 rupees and asked me to withdraw it from the ATM because he had an urgent situation as his mother was going to her village due to an emergency. As a friend, I withdrew the money and gave it to him.

Now I have all the proofs and details to explain to the police, so I emailed all the details to the Bangalore Cyber Cell or the police station where my notice was issued, as mentioned in the acknowledgement given by my bank. However, I did not receive any response. I then tried to contact the investigation officer mentioned in the report. I called several times, keeping a gap of five to six hours out of respect for his time and duties, as they may have many other responsibilities. I also sent him a message on WhatsApp, but there was still no response.

After four to five days, I called again, and this time he picked up the call. He was speaking in the local language, which I did not understand, as I am from Maharashtra and not familiar with the local language of Bangalore. I then started speaking in English, and he told me that I have to come to Bangalore and verify my documents. I explained that for 6000 rupees, it would not be beneficial for me to travel to Bangalore because transportation, food, and stay would cost more than 6000 rupees. He said that he does not know and that I have to come, otherwise he will not issue the No Objection Certificate, and then he ended the call.

This issue may look small, but similar issues are happening everywhere, and no one is noticing them. It feels like “Kare koi aur bhare koi.” Many innocent people face this issue, and it remains unresolved. Because of chain transactions that come into accounts, some people are unable to use their own money. If I travel, I will have to spend more than 6000 rupees to remove the lien. I believe this issue can be resolved through email or online verification, but the investigation officer denied it.

I am also tagging Pushpendra Sir @pushpendrakum and Bangalore Cyber Police @BlrCityPolice . If you could please look into this matter.

Thank you.

🚨 Binance P2P se Bank Account Freeze? Poori Guide + Real Solution (2026)

Bhai aur beheno, agar aap bhi Binance P2P trading karte ho aur suddenly bank account freeze ho gaya hai toh pareshan mat ho. Yeh bahut common problem hai India mein. Innocent log bhi fas jaate hain jab kisi buyer/seller ka paisa kisi fraud case se link hota hai.

Yeh steps follow karo - 

1️⃣ Sabse Pehle Bank Branch Jaao  
   - Freeze ka exact reason, Cyber Crime complaint number, IO naam aur Police Station details lo.  
   - Written notice maang lo.

2️⃣ Saare Proofs Collect Karo (Bahut Important)  
   - Binance P2P complete order history (screenshots)  
   - Buyer/Seller ke saath chat  
   - Payment proof (UPI, bank transfer screenshot)  
   - Bank statement jisme transaction dikhe  
   - Aadhaar, PAN, Binance account details

3️⃣ Binance Support ko turant contact karo  
   - App mein Help section → Submit ticket  
   - Order ID aur proofs attach karo. Woh counterparty ko investigate kar sakte hain.

4️⃣ Cyber Cell mein Representation Daalo  
   - Local Cyber Police Station ya online portal pe jaao.  
   - Detailed application likho ki transaction genuine tha Binance P2P pe hua.  
   - Saare proofs attach karo.  
   - Lawyer (Cyber crime specialist) ki madad le lo - yeh bahut kaam aata hai.

5️⃣ Follow-up karte raho  
   - Har 7-10 din mein bank aur cyber cell ko call/email karo.  
   - Partial release ke liye request kar sakte ho.

Extra Tips jo future mein bacha sakte hain:
• P2P ke liye alag dedicated bank account use karo (savings account mat use karo)
• Sirf verified buyers/sellers ke saath trade karo
• Video verification ya proper KYC maango
• Bahut bade amounts ek baar mein mat trade karo
• Binance P2P risky hai India mein, agar ho sake toh avoid karo

 In March 2026, ahead of the Kerala Assembly elections (polling on 9 April 2026), a 2019 Election Commission of India (ECI) letter redistributed by the Kerala Chief Electoral Officer’s (CEO) office was found to carry the seal of the BJP’s Kerala unit. This sparked a political row, followed by police-directed efforts to remove related social media posts

This takedown action itself became controversial, with critics framing it as an attempt to suppress discussion of an official lapse during an election period, while authorities maintained it was necessary to stop the circulation of a withdrawn and erroneous document that was being used to question the ECI’s credibility.The episode remained a flashpoint in the final stretch of the Kerala campaign, with the ECI treating it as a corrected administrative mistake and the opposition presenting it as evidence of deeper concerns about the poll body’s independence.The letter and the seal
The document was an ECI communication dated 19 March 2019 containing guidelines/FAQs on the publicity of candidates’ criminal antecedents (following a Supreme Court judgment). CPI(M) and Congress shared versions online showing the BJP Kerala unit’s seal. It had been circulated by the Kerala CEO’s office to political parties, District Election Officers, and Returning Officers as part of clarifications around mid-March 2026.thesouthfirst.comKerala CEO / ECI explanation:
It was described as a “purely clerical error.” The BJP Kerala unit had approached the CEO’s office seeking clarification on the (by then revised) 2019 guidelines and submitted a photocopy of the original directive that already bore the party’s seal. Staff overlooked this and redistributed that version. The error was identified; on 21 March a formal withdrawal notice was issued telling recipients to disregard the document. An Assistant Section Officer was suspended pending inquiry. Later, a Deputy CEO and a Section Officer were relieved of election-related duties.livemint.comOpposition parties (CPI(M) and Congress) rejected the clerical-error account. They alleged compromised institutional neutrality, claiming seals were being “casually swapped” and questioning whether the ECI and BJP shared the same “power centre.” Some BJP responses labelled the circulation of the old document as misinformation or a political plot.thewire.inDeletion of posts controversyActing on an ECI directive (under the Model Code of Conduct), the Kerala Police cyber cell issued notices to X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and numerous individual accounts. They demanded removal of posts sharing the letter that carried the BJP seal.  Police argued the content insulted the Election Commission, undermined its integrity and transparency, spread false claims about a rectified clerical error, and risked public order or communal harmony by potentially fuelling political division. Reports indicated hundreds of accounts were flagged (approximately 270 on X, 200 on Facebook, and 90 on Instagram). A stand-up comedian had two of his original Instagram reels removed after anonymous accounts filed copyright complaints using the same generic Turkish-language text, without identifying any allegedly infringed work. It took a Delhi High Court case for Meta to restore both reels. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/RukNwsovEw

But restoration is not the end of the issue. The High Court order does not record that the copyright strikes themselves have been expunged. The questions of removing those strikes and preventing Meta from taking adverse action against Pulkit's page on their basis remain before the Court. (9/10)

This case shows what happens when copyright enforcement becomes the easiest route to getting content removed. A platform says complaints are reviewed and only valid reports are acted upon. Yet two vague complaints were enough to remove content, while repeated appeals produced no reasoned response for months. If the correct decision could be reached once a case entered court, why was it unavailable through the platform's own grievance system?

IFF will continue pushing for meaningful verification of copyright claims, reasoned decisions on appeals within the IT Rules' timelines, and greater transparency around takedowns and reversals. (10/10)

Can we talk about Meta's glasses for a second?

They look like ordinary sunglasses, and the only warning is a tiny LED most people never notice. In just three weeks, we've sent two legal notices to Meta. One is for a man secretly filmed and mocked at a Delhi café. The other is for a woman covertly recorded on her walk home for a "pickup artist's" Instagram content.

Being in public shouldn't mean becoming someone's content without your consent. This is NOT normal.

Here are the two legal notices we sent to Meta over its Ray-Ban smart glasses:

Case 1: Harassment for clout
A man sitting alone at a café was harassed and secretly filmed, and the video was posted to mock him. We're seeking ₹2.05 crore in damages.
Read more: https://t.co/l8nJZDlX3w

Case 2: Stalking as "pickup" content
A woman walking home was covertly recorded to sell "approach classes" on Instagram. She filed a police complaint, and we sent Meta a second notice.
Read more: https://t.co/GXoD9IHFZd

If you've ever been filmed like this without your consent, you're not alone, and it's not okay. Please share this with someone who should know.

Phone jammers 👇🏽👇🏽

quotedTweet.text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

text:
There is a crucial difference between an internet shutdown and a phone jammer. An internet shutdown requires a written order under the Telecommunications Act. A jammer is a radio transmitter that can cut voice calls, SMS and mobile data for everyone within its range. So who gives the Delhi Police the power to switch one on? (1/10)
Read More: https://t.co/kU0KOf2fOY

On 8 September, IFF filed three RTIs with the Delhi Police. We are seeking records on every jammer it possesses, the permissions and procurement documents, the officers authorised to deploy them, the applicable SOPs and deployment registers, and the specific records concerning Jantar Mantar on 20 and 22 July. We have also asked for the records behind the Satya Niketan denial. (9/10)

The question is not whether telecommunications can ever be restricted. Indian law already provides a framework for temporary suspension of services. The question is whether a separate, less visible mechanism can bypass those safeguards and cut communications without the written order, publication, review and accountability that accompany a lawful shutdown. IFF will publish the Delhi Police's replies, including any silence, and continue seeking clarity on who can jam communications, for what purpose and under what law. (10/10)

Support our work: https://t.co/qSG7IzUpIX

This matters because the Delhi Police has powers to regulate public assemblies under the Delhi Police Act, and urgent powers exist under Section 163 of the BNSS. But neither provision gives the police a power to jam telecommunications. In *Anuradha Bhasin*, the Supreme Court held that telecommunications can be suspended only through the legally prescribed framework. Section 163 cannot become a substitute for that framework. (6/10)

There is also a basic rights problem. RML Hospital received injured police personnel after clashes near Jantar Mantar on 22 July, and RML and Lady Hardinge are within roughly two kilometres of the protest site. A jammer that cuts ordinary phone service can also cut a person's ability to call 112, a hospital or family. It can also prevent journalists and citizens from transmitting what is happening at a public assembly. (7/10)

Ray-Ban Meta glasses struck again. A woman walking home alone was secretly recorded by a man who approached her, then posted the footage on Instagram alongside similar clips of him doing this to other women, as part of "pickup" content.

She's filed a police complaint for stalking and voyeurism. IFF is assisting her with a legal notice to the creator, Instagram, and Meta, the second such notice against Meta in India.

This isn't a one off. It's a design problem.
Read more about it: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

A woman was followed, stopped on a dark street, secretly recorded through Ray-Ban Meta glasses and turned into an Instagram “pickup” reel that reached over 23 lakh views. Now, our legal notice seeks accountability from both him and Meta. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/x5Gzp2NFF0

The legal notice therefore puts Meta on notice not merely as the platform hosting the video, but as the designer, developer, manufacturer, marketer and seller of the glasses. It alleges negligence and product liability, arguing that Meta knew about the pattern of misuse but continued selling the device without an effective way for non-users or people being recorded to report that misuse. (9/10)

The notice seeks removal of every copy, preservation and disclosure of evidence, suspension of monetisation, an account of profits, an apology, and ₹2.05 crore in compensatory and exemplary damages. This case raises a larger question: when a company makes a camera that can be worn like ordinary glasses, who protects the person being recorded? Privacy cannot depend on whether the person being filmed has an Instagram account. (10/10)
